column1: # The non-git host state of THIS installation: everything a rebuilt server needs
# that the repository alone cannot supply.
# `instructions/reproducible-from-git.md` requires exactly this file by its own
# words -- "Host state that must NOT be in git is enumerated instead ... what it
# is, where it goes, what permissions it needs, and the command that verifies
# it" -- and until now no such enumeration existed. The meteorite test proves the
# REPOSITORY rebuilds a host; it says nothing about the credentials, the state
# database, or the mission history, and a correct rebuild that loses those is
# still a loss. Operator order, Telegram 2734: back the set up to his Drive
# «щоб я потім хоч десяток серверів міг підняти».
# Format: path<TAB>kind<TAB>what<TAB>mode<TAB>verify-command<TAB>in-backup
#   path            absolute path on this host. Never a value, only a location:
#                   this file is tracked, so a secret's CONTENT must never reach
#                   it (Hard Floor 4).
#   kind            classification token, no whitespace.
#   what            one line on why a new server needs it.
#   mode            the octal permission the path must carry.
#   verify-command  a single shell line, exit 0 iff the row holds. It checks the
#                   permission too, because a key restored world-readable is a
#                   different defect from a key not restored at all. Run every
#                   row with `bun tools/backup-host-state.ts --check`; that is
#                   also the executable half of cutover gate F, whose current
#                   reading of this file checks only its shape.
#   in-backup       yes | no. `no` has two distinct reasons, and both are
#                   deliberate: either the repository already reproduces the
#                   path, so copying it off-host would only create a second
#                   thing to keep in sync (the two rendered rows at the bottom),
#                   or copying it would be a defect in itself -- the backup
#                   passphrase must never travel inside the archive it opens.
# Every cell must be non-empty; an unknown value is a FAIL, never a blank.
# RESTORING, after the meteorite -- the enumeration is only half the obligation;
# the other half is that someone can act on it from the repository alone:
#   1. Clone this repository. The archive lives in the Drive folder named by
#      instance/params.yaml `backup.drive_folder_id`, reachable with the key at
#      `backup.service_account_key` -- or, when that key is itself gone, with the
#      operator's own Google session on that shared drive.
#   2. `bun tools/backup-host-state.ts --verify [--passphrase-file <path>]`
#      proves the newest archive restores BEFORE anything is trusted to it.
#   3. Unpack it. Every member sits under `files/` at its absolute path minus the
#      leading slash, `manifest.tsv` records the bytes and file count each was
#      archived with, and the `mode` column below is the permission each must be
#      restored with. `--check` then re-runs every verify-command.
#   4. The backup passphrase. `backup.encryption: operator-passphrase` means the
#      OPERATOR holds the authoritative copy in his own store, and that copy is
#      what opens the archives after a meteorite. Its VALUE is nowhere in the
#      repository, in params, inside the archive or on the Drive, and losing his
#      copy loses every encrypted archive -- which is why the alternative mode
#      (`none`) exists and announces itself on every run.
#      A second, WORKING copy does sit on this host, because the hourly timer
#      runs unattended and cannot be handed a passphrase interactively. It is
#      enumerated below like any other host state -- its path, its 0600 mode and
#      its verify-command -- and it is the one row that must NEVER be restored
#      from the archive, because it is `in-backup: no` precisely so the archive
#      does not carry its own key. After a rebuild, the operator writes it back
#      from his copy; nothing else can.
# One property of row 3 is deliberate and worth naming once: the service-account
# key is the credential the backup tool authenticates to Drive with, and it is
# also inside the archive. Recovering it from the archive therefore needs the
# operator's own browser session on the Drive, not the key. He ordered that
# explicitly ("той самий ключ, який ти використовуєш для доступу до цього Google
# Диска"), and it is sound -- he is the second factor.
/root/.ssh/id_github_vova
column3: GitHub deploy key; without it a rebuilt host cannot clone this repository at all, so it is the first thing the meteorite path needs

column1: /root/.config/bpa/orchestrator.env
column3: Orchestrator and Telegram-daemon environment: bot token, chat binding, lease and watchdog values

column1: /root/.config/bpa/oauth/gcp-sa-bpapro-agents.json
column3: GCP service-account key; the agent's Google Drive credential, and the one this backup tool itself authenticates with

column1: /root/.config/bpa/oauth/google.env
column3: Google API client configuration for the agent's Drive and Sheets access

column1: /root/.config/bpa/oauth/qbo.env
column3: QuickBooks API credentials used by the product-side integration work

column1: /root/.claude/.credentials.json
column3: Claude CLI credential; minted by an interactive login that is operator-only, so a lost copy costs an operator session

column1: /root/.codex/auth.json
column3: Codex CLI credential; same operator-only interactive login, and today the fleet's working provider

column1: /root/.codex/config.toml
column3: Codex CLI configuration as tuned on this host

column1: /root/bpa-dev-infrastructure/orchestrator/runtime.env
column3: Per-host launcher configuration (ports, chat binding, provider and model choice); gitignored by design, its tracked contract is runtime.env.example

column1: /root/bpa-dev-infrastructure/runtime/state.db
column3: The v3 durable core state database: missions, lanes, leases. This is the system's memory of what it was doing

column1: /root/.config/bpa/orchestrator-state.sqlite
column3: The v1 orchestrator state database, retained: the pre-cutover history nothing else holds

column1: /root/bpa-dev-infrastructure/orchestrator/runtime
column3: Ops journal plus every lane task and terminal report; the record of what the fleet did and why

column1: /root/.local/state/bpa-dev-infrastructure/evidence
column3: Durable evidence under XDG_STATE_HOME, including the latest meteorite result

column1: /root/bpa-dev-infrastructure/instance/decisions/inbox.jsonl
column3: Raw inbound operator messages. Deliberately never committed (it may carry credentials), and the only complete copy of his verbatim words before triage

column1: /root/.local/bin/orch-fleet-nudge.sh
column3: Installed by bootstrap from the tracked source; reproduced by re-running the installer, so it is enumerated but not archived

column1: /etc/systemd/system/bpa-orchestrator.service
column3: Representative of the rendered unit set; bootstrap/install.sh regenerates every unit from bootstrap/units/*.in, so archiving them would only create drift

column1: /root/.config/bpa/backup-passphrase
column3: Working copy of the GPG passphrase the hourly backup encrypts with; the operator holds the authoritative copy, so this one is never restored from the archive -- and never rides inside it, or the archive would carry its own key
